lead: I try to understand neural systems because I know how profoundly they can change a life—and how much remains unexplained when they do.
introduction: I’m studying data science and philosophy at NYU, with research interests spanning machine learning, neural computation, and biology. Those interests developed through coursework, but their urgency came from a severe illness that began at the beginning of college. What started as a search for answers about my own health grew into a broader commitment: to develop the technical understanding needed to help people whose suffering we still struggle to explain.

sections.title: Before the questions became personal
paragraphs: Tennis was a large part of my life. I played first singles on an elite team at Northern Highlands, and during the COVID lockdown I often spent six hours a day on court. Training gave my days structure, and physical effort was something I could depend on.

I began to have severe health issues at the beginning of my sophomore year. Activities that had once been routine became inaccessible. I lost the physical capacity I had depended on, and long stretches of illness narrowed the world around me.

It took over a year to begin understanding what was happening. After extensive investigation, we learned that the problem was neurological, involving the neural circuits that regulate the gastrointestinal tract. Investigations had found no structural explanation for the severity of the symptoms. Yet during episodes, I experienced pain and nausea more intense than anything I had previously known.

That recognition gave us a direction. We sought out specialists in neurogastroenterology, hoping that identifying the system involved would bring us closer to an explanation. But even within specialist care, much remained a black box. We could recognize that neural function was disrupted and observe how symptoms responded to treatment, without being able to identify precisely what had changed in the circuits or why. Knowing where the problem lay was still far from understanding how it worked.

I came to see a parallel with artificial neural networks: we can observe a system’s outputs and influence its behavior while still struggling to explain the internal processes responsible. In my own case, the distance between identifying a neurological disorder and understanding its mechanism had immediate consequences for how we could approach treatment.

My care required working through that uncertainty. We used the information available, worked carefully, and tried to reduce the symptoms and periods of pain. Over time, we made immense progress. Treatment made the condition manageable, and I remain deeply grateful for the persistence and care that helped make that possible.

But the improvement left questions I could not put aside. The year before becoming ill, I had been in the best physical condition of my life. Now there were periods when I could barely get out of bed, let alone train or play tennis. How could such a profound change occur without a prior history or a structural explanation on imaging? What had changed in the system, and why was it so difficult to identify?

Those questions opened a further search. I wanted to understand how neural circuits could become so profoundly disrupted, what responses to treatment might reveal about their mechanisms, and how computational tools could help investigate problems that remained difficult to answer clinically. The distance between what I was experiencing and what we could explain became a reason to keep learning—and to develop the technical skills to investigate further.

sections.title: Finding a direction
paragraphs: During that period, I also began exploring my roots and reading philosophical texts that became personally meaningful to me. Questions about suffering, identity, and consciousness had become immediate parts of my life. Reading gave me ways to examine them and drew me further toward the science of experience: how perception arises, how a sense of self develops, and how changes in a nervous system can transform someone’s world.

I became interested in bringing science and philosophy into conversation. Neuroscience and computation offered ways to investigate mechanisms; philosophy helped me think about what those explanations could tell us about experience and what questions remained open. That connection drew me toward philosophy of mind and continues to shape the work I pursue.

My ambitions changed during this time. I came to see research and engineering as the contribution I wanted to make—using the advanced technical tools of our time to develop a deeper understanding and turn it into help for as many people as possible.

sections.title: How that became my work
paragraphs: For long stretches of the illness, joining a lab or taking an internship was beyond what my health allowed. Working independently gave me a way to keep learning and build experience at a pace I could sustain. With public datasets, published research, and a single GPU, I began reproducing models, designing analyses, and developing experiments around the questions that interested me.

My coursework in machine learning provided a practical starting point. Working with C. elegans gave me a nervous system I could begin to study computationally, connecting its wiring diagram to cellular properties and measured activity. As I learned more, my interests developed around several recurring questions.

One is how the structure of a nervous system relates to what it does. My connectome and neural-control projects examine how much measured activity can be explained by wiring, physical proximity, and cell identity. The MICrONS dendritic work approaches a related question at a smaller scale: whether the arrangement of inputs along a dendrite carries information beyond the geometry of the surrounding cells. These projects have taught me to turn broad questions into comparisons that can distinguish competing explanations.

Another is how neural function changes so dramatically across states. My experience of illness made that question personal, and treatment deepened my interest in reversibility. Anesthesia and sleep offered ways to ask how a nervous system can enter a profoundly different state and return. My reading also led toward genetic, mitochondrial, and myelination mechanisms that could affect function without producing an obvious structural explanation.

A third is what we can read from neural signals and make useful. LibriBrain brought me into MEG analysis and the challenge of extracting information from noisy recordings. The wrist-EMG handwriting work explores how signals associated with intended movement can support communication, and how adapting a model to an individual changes its performance.

Across these projects, I have developed experience working with complex biological data, reproducing published systems, training and adapting models, and examining what a result actually depends on. Some promising findings changed substantially under closer testing. Learning to trace those changes has become an important part of how I work.

My broader projects in molecular prediction, clinical data, and robotics have given me opportunities to extend that toolkit and explore other problems where computation could be useful. The questions connecting my work remain close to where I began.

sections.title: What I want to contribute
paragraphs: I am now well enough to pursue opportunities that illness previously put out of reach. I want to bring the technical experience and independence I developed during that time into a research team, learn from colleagues, and contribute to work that benefits from sustained collaboration.

I’m particularly interested in research and research engineering involving neural interfaces, neural data, and machine learning for biology. I enjoy problems that require moving between a scientific question and the practical work of building something that can test it.

Illness changed the life I expected to have and gave lasting purpose to the work I want to do. My goal is to use machine learning, neuroscience, computation, and philosophy to tackle the hardest problems I can contribute to solving—and help make the suffering people experience more bearable.
